spatial_claims.claim: Solid AB has base parallelogram EH and perpendicular height AE; solid CD has base parallelogram NQ and perpendicular height CN
Auxiliary solid FO is constructed on the same base EH as AB but with height equal to CN
Solids AB and FO share the same base EH, so by 11.25 (cutting the taller at the height of the shorter gives a piece equal to the shorter by 11.29/11.31), their ratio equals AE:CN
Solids FO and CD have the same height CN, so by 11.32 their ratio equals base EH : base NQ
Same auxiliary solid FO (base EH, height CN) is reconstructed for the converse
AB and FO share base EH, ratio AB:FO = AE:CN (same spatial relationship as Step 3)
FO and CD share height CN, ratio FO:CD = EH:NQ (same spatial relationship as Step 4)

configuration_map: Three parallelepipedal solids are in play: (1) AB with base EH and height AE, (2) CD with base NQ and height CN, (3) auxiliary FO with base EH and height CN. Solid FO serves as a bridge: it shares its base with AB (enabling comparison via 11.25, same-base ratio equals height ratio) and shares its height with CD (enabling comparison via 11.32, same-height ratio equals base ratio). The three solids are independent constructions; FO is placed on the same base plane as AB. No point or solid is claimed to be simultaneously in two incompatible positions.
pass_reason: The proof is primarily proportional/algebraic, using Book 5 proportion theory to combine two ratio relationships. The spatial claims are limited and mutually consistent: (1) FO shares base EH with AB, (2) FO shares height CN with CD. These two claims are independent and non-contradictory. The construction of FO as a bridge solid linking AB and CD through shared dimensions is a standard and valid technique. No angle decompositions, betweenness claims, or interior/exterior claims are made that could generate spatial contradictions.
